issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An admitted image attachment failed to hydrate when the same turn was **sandboxed** and the workspace exposed
`prepareTurnAttachments` (the file-transfer workspace service). That turn logged `Native image: failed to load`, loaded
zero images, and never read through the sandbox bridge. Either condition alone worked.

## Why This Change Was Made

`loadMediaRef` already documents the rule — "Admitted managed originals belong to Gateway; staged and discovered paths stay
sandboxed" — but the `gatewayAttachment` test did not honour the staged half:

- with a binding present it became true even for a **staged** ref, so `sandbox` was dropped;
- the local roots then narrowed to the media directory, and the staged copy lives under the sandbox root, so
  `loadWebMediaRaw` raised `path-not-allowed` and the failure was swallowed into a log line.

The staged flag now survives the fact-to-ref conversion (`mediaFactToImageRef` carries `staged: fact.staged === true`,
typed on `MediaFileRef`), and `gatewayAttachment` excludes staged refs, so a sandbox-staged copy keeps the sandbox reader
that produced it. Gateway-owned originals (`media://` facts without a staged twin) behave exactly as before.

## User Impact

Sandboxed turns that also use the file-transfer workspace now hydrate their staged images instead of silently dropping
them, so the model receives the picture the transcript says was attached. Non-sandboxed turns and Gateway-owned originals
are unchanged.

## Evidence

New case in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/images.media-refs.test.ts`, modelled on the issue's route matrix: a tiny
PNG staged under `media/inbound/`, a sandbox at that root, and `registerAgentWorkspaceAccess` supplying a bridge plus
`prepareTurnAttachments`. It asserts the image loads.

Red on base behaviour: reverting only the two production files fails with
`expected undefined to match object { type: 'image', … }` (`1 failed | 14 skipped`); with the change the file reports
`15 passed`.

- `oxlint` on all three touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- Test lines carry an allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/native-image-staged-sandbox.txt`.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

comment.body:
@clawsweeper re-review

**P2 finding — you were right, and the fix is now narrower.** `stageSandboxMedia` also marks Gateway-owned copies as
staged (media/remote-cache), so blanket `ref.staged !== true` sent those cached paths through the sandbox bridge and, with
`workspaceOnly`, narrowed host reads away from `getMediaDir()`. The condition now distinguishes the two producers:

```ts
// Staged copies have two producers: the sandbox staging step (a path the sandbox
// bridge owns) and Gateway's own remote cache under the media directory. Only the
// sandbox-owned copy keeps the sandbox reader; the cached one stays on Gateway.
const stagedInMediaDir = ref.staged === true && isPathInside(getMediaDir(), ref.resolved);
const gatewayAttachment = attachment && (ref.staged !== true || stagedInMediaDir) && Boolean(…);
```

Both routes are covered now, as you asked:

- `hydrates a sandbox-staged path when the workspace also prepares turn attachments` — sandbox-owned copy, the regression
  this PR fixes (red on base: `expected undefined to match object { type: 'image' }`).
- `keeps a Gateway remote-cache staged copy on the Gateway reader` — `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`-rooted `media/remote-cache`
  path with a sandbox and `workspaceOnly` present, which must stay on the Gateway reader. It passes before and after, so
  it guards the route instead of re-proving the fix.

Whole file: `16 passed`. `oxlint` 0/0.

On the proof item: the loader is the shipped path for this behaviour (`detectAndLoadPromptImages` is what the embedded
runner calls before a turn), and both cases drive it with real files on disk plus a real sandbox bridge. I cannot produce a
Gateway/CLI trace for this specific combination here — the same CLI limits reported on #194396 apply (no command-path
delivery, no real model credential) — but the file-level test exercises the same entry point the runner uses, including the
workspace binding that triggered the bug.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A follow-up message queued while a run is active is dropped when `/stop` is used. The dispatcher mirrors the stop's
command exchange into the transcript, and the queued follow-up's replay admission then resolves the **command row** as
the current turn, refuses with `Persisted user turn changed before replay admission`, and the message is never answered.

Reproduced with the reporter's fixture (`extensions`-free, real session manager + real transcript): on `main` the queued
follow-up ends with `0` model calls and that error; with this change it is answered.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/agents/sessions/session-manager-current-turn.ts` decides which transcript entries the current-turn walk may step
over. It already treats context metadata, compaction markers and runtime/system custom messages as traversable because
they are not model-facing turns. A delivered command exchange is the same kind of row — a transcript mirror of the
dispatcher's reply — but it was not listed, so the walk stopped on it.

The fix marks rows whose `idempotencyKey` is `command-input:*` or `command-reply:*` as traversable. Nothing else changes:
real user turns still stop the walk, and the admission still requires the prepared user message to match exactly.

## User Impact

A queued follow-up survives `/stop`: it is persisted once and gets answered instead of silently disappearing behind a
generic "couldn't finish this reply". Commands that are not mirrored (`/new` etc. still write their exchange the same
way) behave the same, and no transcript bytes change.

## Evidence

Reporter's fixture, run with `node scripts/test-projects.mts <file>`:

| case | base | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| no interposed write (control) | answered | answered |
| Workshop notice interposed (control, #181473) | answered | answered |
| **`/stop` exchange interposed** | `Persisted user turn changed before replay admission`, 0 model calls | 1 model call, `FOLLOWUP_ANSWERED` |

- Base: `2 failed | 4 passed` (both reader modes fail on the interposed case). Fixed: `6 passed`.
- Neighbours: `attempt-session-replay.test.ts` 61 passed; `session-manager-bounded.test.ts` 28 passed;
  `session-manager-async-entries.test.ts` 9 passed.
- `oxlint`: 0 warnings, 0 errors. The new test file carries an allocation in
  `config/test-lines-allocations/stop-exchange-replay-admission.txt`.

### Why there is no gateway-level trace here

I built the full isolated stack and tried to drive the reported race, then stopped when the attempt could not reach
the state the report describes. What works, and what does not:

- **Works**: an isolated gateway from a built worktree (`gateway run --port 3099` with a `--profile`-isolated config,
  `/health` 200) plus the repo's mock model server (`scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs`) really does run agent turns —
  `openclaw --profile … agent -m "…"` returns the mock's marker.
- **Does not reach the race**: `openclaw agent -m "/stop"` is delivered as an ordinary user message, not as a slash
  command. In my runs the long first turn reported `aborted: false` and `stopReason: "stop"`, and the `/stop` call was
  queued and answered like any other turn. Without an actual command-path stop there is no command exchange mirrored
  into the transcript, which is precisely the precondition this fix changes.
- Earlier notes in this PR cited process-supervisor failures for e2e; those were real, but they are not the reason this
  trace is missing. The accurate reason is the one above: the CLI agent channel does not exercise the command path.

What a reviewer can run instead, given a channel that delivers commands (the report used Telegram): queue a follow-up
during an active turn, send `/stop`, and confirm the queued message still reaches a model request instead of failing with
`Persisted user turn changed before replay admission`. The reporter's fixture in this PR covers the same predicate without
a channel: it fails on base with that error and passes with the change.

## Scope

One production file (the traversal predicate), the reporter's regression test registered next to
`attempt-session-replay.test.ts` in `test/vitest/vitest.database-worker-core-paths.mjs`, and the allocation file.

and its evidence.

### Gateway-level proof: what a CI-shaped test would need

I could not produce this here (no provider endpoint on this machine), but the pieces are in the repo:

- `test/helpers/openclaw-test-instance.ts` starts a real Gateway with isolated state without Playwright

- `scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs` is an OpenAI-compatible mock with `MOCK_RESPONSE_CHUNK_DELAY_MS`, which keeps a turn

- With those two, a `*.real-gateway.e2e.test.ts` can assert: first turn streaming -> second `chat.send` queues ->
  `/stop` -> the queued message receives an assistant reply (base: user row only, no reply).

there is no fixture to copy for this yet.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`message` action `thread-reply` silently dropped a `buffer` (base64 / data-URL) attachment. The reply posted as text, the
receipt reported `kind: "text"`, and nothing failed — so an agent that posted a PDF report through `thread-reply` + `buffer`
saw success while the thread only got the text. Passing the same file as `media` worked, which is what made the loss
invisible.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `thread-reply` branch reads `media`, `path` and `filePath`, but never looks at `buffer`. The tool schema advertises
`buffer` as a generic attachment field, so an agent has no signal that this action ignores it.

Rather than adding a second upload path, this takes the option the report offers and mirrors the sibling `upload-file`
guard, which already refuses buffer attachments and points at `send`. `thread-reply` now fails the same way when a buffer
is present and no file source was given:

```
Use action: "send" for base64 buffer attachments; thread-reply requires filePath, path, or media.
```

The losing side effect becomes a loud error under the caller's control, and `send` remains the one owner of buffer
uploads. `thread-reply` with `media`/`path`/`filePath` is unchanged.

## User Impact

A caller that passes a buffer to `thread-reply` now gets an actionable error instead of a text-only post that looks
successful. Nothing else changes: media replies, thread creation and every other action keep their behaviour.

## Evidence

`extensions/discord/src/actions/handle-action.test.ts` gains a case driving the real handler through the existing
`threadAction`/`runAction` harness with `{ threadId, message, buffer, filename }` and asserting the rejection message.

Red on base behaviour: reverting only `handle-action.guild-admin.ts` fails the new case (`1 failed | 33 skipped`); with
the change the file reports `34 passed`.

- `oxlint` on both touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- Test lines carry an allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/discord-thread-reply-buffer.txt`.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

comment.body:
@clawsweeper re-review

On the proof item, reporting exactly how far this can be driven and where it stops rather than claiming a run I did not
make.

**What I verified about the shipped surface.** `openclaw message thread reply` has no `--buffer` flag (`--message`,
`--media`, thread/target options only), so a base64 `buffer` cannot be passed from the CLI at all. It can only arrive
through the `message` tool schema, i.e. through an agent tool call. The repo's mock model server
(`scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs`) returns canned text and does not emit tool calls, and this environment has no real
model credential — so I cannot execute the tool-call path myself.

**What the fix guarantees regardless of that path.** The guard runs in the `thread-reply` branch *before* any Discord
request is built: when `media`/`path`/`filePath` are all absent and `buffer` is present, it throws and the handler never
posts. That is exactly the property the report asks for — no text-only post that looks successful — and it is asserted at
the handler boundary the action owns, in the same place the sibling `upload-file` guard is asserted.

**How a maintainer can capture it**, given a real model or a scripted tool call plus a Discord bot: call the `message`
tool with `{action:"thread-reply", channel:"discord", threadId, message, buffer, filename, mimeType}` for both raw base64
and a `data:` URL; each should fail with `Use action: "send" for base64 buffer attachments; thread-reply requires filePath,
path, or media.` and post nothing. The control, `{action:"thread-reply", …, media:"/tmp/report.pdf"}`, should post with
`parts[0].kind: "media"`.

If you would rather have the buffer actually uploaded rather than refused, say so and I will take that path instead — the
report accepts either outcome.

issue.title: fix(agents): keep a decimal dot inside the block while the stream is open

labels.name: repo-535d150f

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

With block streaming on and a small chunk floor, a dot inside a number ended a block: `| 内存 | 11.65 GiB |` was
delivered as `| 内存 | 11.` plus a paragraph break plus `65 GiB |`, and the reply coalescer joined the two with `\n\n`.
The same happened to `2026.11.2` and `10.0.0.12`. The transcript held `11.65` as one token; only the delivered text was
corrupted.

## Why This Change Was Made

`EmbeddedBlockChunker` finds a sentence boundary with `/[.!?](?=\s|$)/g` over the **current buffer**
(`src/agents/embedded-agent-block-chunker.ts`). While the stream is open, the end of that buffer is not the end of the
message, so a freshly arrived `.` in `11.65` matched `$` and closed the block immediately; with `minChars: 1` the
three-character fragment was then emitted.

The preferred-break picker now knows whether the drain is final and only treats end-of-buffer as a sentence end when it
is:

- `#pickPreferredBreakIndex` takes a `final` flag;
- an open drain matches `/[.!?](?=\s)/`, a final drain keeps `/[.!?](?=\s|$)/`;
- the forced-tail call site passes `true`, and `#pickBreakIndex` forwards its own `force`.

A dot followed by a digit no longer matches at all while streaming, so `11.65`, `2026.11.2` and `10.0.0.12` stay inside
one block. Real sentence ends still break: the next delta brings the space that the lookahead needs, and the final drain
still ends on `$`.

Out of scope, recorded deliberately: the coalescer still re-joins adjacent blocks with the paragraph joiner
(`dispatch-from-config.payloads`). With this fix a decimal is never split, so that path no longer corrupts numbers, but
re-joining with the consumed separator is a separate change in a different owner and is not attempted here.

## User Impact

Delivered block-streamed text stays byte-identical to the model output for numbers, versions, IP addresses and
identifiers that contain a dot. Paragraph, newline and sentence breaking for ordinary prose is unchanged; the existing
chunker suites still pass.

## Evidence

New case in `src/agents/embedded-agent-block-chunker.test.ts` streams the reported Markdown table one character at a
time (the worst case a provider delta can produce) and asserts:

- the concatenated chunks equal the source exactly;
- no non-final chunk ends with `.`.

Red on base behaviour: reverting only `embedded-agent-block-chunker.ts` fails with `expected true to be false` (a chunk
does end with the decimal dot); with the change the file reports `28 passed`.

- `oxlint` on both touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- Test lines carry an allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/block-chunker-decimal-boundary.txt`.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

comment.body:
@clawsweeper re-review

On the proof item, being explicit rather than claiming a trace I cannot capture.

**What the current evidence is.** The new case streams the reported Markdown table one character at a time through the
real `EmbeddedBlockChunker` — the worst boundary a provider delta can produce — and asserts the concatenated chunks equal
the source with no non-final chunk ending in `.`. Red on base: `expected true to be false`; with the change the file
reports `28 passed`. That covers the chunker owner the report names.

**Why no channel trace is attached.** Delivery through Gateway/channel cannot be produced in this environment:

- Gateway e2e cannot run here: the built runtime is available, but e2e tests fail in the process supervisor with
  `service child cleanup identity lost: native owner closed without kernel descendant extinction` (reproduced with
  `test/gateway-restart-lane.e2e.test.ts`, which fails before reaching this change).
- Isolated-gateway RPC auth does not resolve: `gateway.auth.mode: "none"` still answers `token_missing`, and an accepted
  token answers `token_mismatch`, although `src/gateway/auth.ts` returns ok for `mode: "none"`.

**How to capture it.** Set the reporter's config (`blockStreamingDefault: "on"`, `blockStreamingBreak: "text_end"`,
`chunking`/`coalesce` at `minChars: 1`, `idleMs: 900`), have an agent answer with a table containing `11.65 GiB`, and
compare the delivered block text with the transcript: the delivered text should be byte-identical, where before it
contained `11.` + a paragraph break + `65`. The chunker-level regression in this PR is the same path without the channel
hop, which is why I consider it sufficient — but I cannot attach the channel trace myself.

`agents.entries.<id>.thinkingDefault` is documented as the per-agent default thinking level, and its bullet links to
[thinking resolution order](/tools/thinking#resolution-order), but that section never covered subagent spawns. A reader
therefore expected `thinkingDefault: "off"` on a specialist to apply when `main` spawns it with `sessions_spawn`, and the
child silently ran at the caller's level instead. The full spawn precedence order was written down nowhere.

## Why This Change Was Made

This takes the report's second option — keep the behaviour, document it — because the inheritance is intentional:
`docs/tools/subagents/tool-reference.md` already states that native sub-agents inherit the caller's turn and that only ACP
spawns apply the target's `thinkingDefault`.

New `Subagent spawns` subsection under the resolution order in `docs/tools/thinking.md` lists every step of the chain,
checked against `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn-thinking.ts`:

1. an explicit `sessions_spawn.thinking` argument;
2. the requester's `agents.entries.*.subagents.thinking`;
3. the target's `agents.entries.*.subagents.thinking`;
4. `agents.defaults.subagents.thinking`;
5. the caller's own selected level, only when that level was chosen explicitly (`callerThinkingExplicit !== false`).

It also records the two consequences the report needed: the first resolved value is saved on the child session as its
initial `thinkingLevel`, so it outranks the child's own `thinkingDefault` on later turns; with none of the five, the child
uses its own model default. ACP spawns additionally apply the target's `thinkingDefault` then its per-model
`params.thinking`. The section names both entry points (`subagent-spawn-plan.ts` for native,
`acp-spawn-runtime.ts` for ACP) so a future change to the chain has an obvious doc to update.

The `thinkingDefault` bullet in `docs/gateway/config-agents/entries-and-multi-agent.md` now says which case it does *not*
cover and links to the new section, and names the target-side `subagents.thinking` workaround — including the caveat that
a requester-side `subagents.thinking` still wins.

## User Impact

Docs only; no behaviour change. Someone configuring a specialist agent now sees why the child ignored
`thinkingDefault`, what to set instead, and every condition of the chain that decides it.

## Evidence

- `pnpm format:docs:check` → `Docs formatting clean (1421 files)`.
- `pnpm lint:docs` → `Summary: 0 issues in 0 files`.
- Every step, the persistence consequence and both entry points are quoted from
  `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn-thinking.ts:12-30` and its callers (`subagent-spawn-plan.ts:21,175-188`,
  `acp-spawn-runtime.ts:103-117`) rather than from the report.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

Both findings were correct; fixed.

**P2 — ACP has its own order.** I checked the caller (`acp-spawn-runtime.ts`): it passes only `cfg`, `targetAgentConfig`

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a subagent completion finished successfully but produced no visible reply, the announce classifier returned
`disposition: "retryable"`. Nothing about a settled reply can change on a retry, so the same completion was re-admitted
every time the gateway dedupe entry expired: the report measured 170, 164 and 138 warning records for three image
completions, at a median interval of about two seconds, each logging
`Subagent completion direct announce failed for session image_generate:<task>`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`missingVisibleReplyResult` now reports `disposition: "permanent_failure"` for a completed run instead of `"retryable"`
(`src/agents/subagents/announce/subagent-announce-direct-response.ts`).

This connects an existing producer to an existing consumer rather than adding a mechanism:

- `SubagentDeliveryDisposition` already declares `"permanent_failure"`
  (`src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-registry-read.types.ts`), and the delivery record persists it
  (`subagent-delivery-state.ts`: the durable projection carries `{ status, disposition, suspendedAt }`).
- `subagent-registry-lifecycle-announce-cleanup.ts` already handles exactly this pair — `reason === "visible_reply_missing"`
  with `disposition === "permanent_failure"` suspends the pending final delivery, records `lastDropReason`, and stops
  re-arming the announcement.
- The outcome is genuinely terminal: `requesterCompletedSuccessfully` derives from the completed run's announce record
  (`directAnnounceRecord?.status === "ok"`, with `requireTerminalContent: true`), not from a partial stream. A reply that
  arrives later in the same run would not be a `visible_reply_missing` case.

The user-visible effect is that the retry storm stops and the completion is recorded once as undeliverable instead of
repeating until the dedupe window rolls over.

## User Impact

A completion that cannot produce a visible reply is recorded as a permanent outcome instead of being retried
indefinitely. Conversation flow is no longer delayed by repeated completion handling for an old image task, and the
warning log stops growing. Successful deliveries, `session_queued` handoffs, `intentional_non_delivery`, and
in-flight `retryable` failures are unchanged.

## Evidence

`src/agents/subagents/announce/subagent-announce-delivery.test.ts` already exercises this path for the in-process route;
its assertion now requires the recorded disposition.

| case | base | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| completed run, no visible reply, in-process route | `record.disposition: expected 'retryable' to deeply equal 'permanent_failure'` (1 failed / 109 passed) | `110 passed` |

- `oxlint` on both touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- The test file is already above its line cap, so the assertion is written as a one-line change and adds no counted line;
  `config/test-lines-allocations/subagent-missing-reply-permanent.txt` records the allocation.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

comment.body:
@clawsweeper re-review

Addressed two of the three items; the third is the proof item I cannot produce here.

**P1 — continuations were being made permanent.** You were right, and the bug was mine. The `message_tool_only`
branch reaches `missingVisibleReplyResult` *because* `yielded` or `continuationPending` is set, so my change would have
turned a live continuation into a permanent outcome. The call now classifies as permanent only when the response is
genuinely settled:

```ts
return missingVisibleReplyResult(
  requesterCompletedSuccessfully &&
    directAnnounceResult?.meta?.yielded !== true &&
    directAnnounceResult?.meta?.continuationPending !== true,
);
```

Yielded and continuing responses therefore keep their previous `retryable` classification and the requester-settle path
still schedules the next attempt.

**P2 — allocation removed.** `config/test-lines-allocations/subagent-missing-reply-permanent.txt` is deleted; the test
change replaces one line with one line, so it needs no credit. The diff is now the one production line plus that
one-line assertion.

**Still open — real behavior proof.** I could not produce a Gateway trace after dedupe expiry in this environment, and
the two reasons are reproducible rather than assumed:

- Gateway e2e cannot run here: the built runtime is available, but e2e tests fail in the process supervisor with
  `service child cleanup identity lost: native owner closed without kernel descendant extinction` (reproduced with
  `test/gateway-restart-lane.e2e.test.ts`, unrelated to this change).
- Isolated-gateway RPC auth does not resolve: with `gateway.auth.mode: "none"` the RPC still answers `token_missing`,
  and a token the gateway accepts answers `token_mismatch`, although `src/gateway/auth.ts` returns `ok` for `mode: "none"`.

To reproduce the fix elsewhere: start a Gateway with the mock provider (`scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs`), let a
`image_generate`-style completion settle without a visible reply, and confirm the completion is announced once with
`disposition: permanent_failure` and is not re-admitted after the dedupe window — versus repeated
`Subagent completion direct announce failed` warnings before the change.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When Muse's provider stream dies mid-reply, MSP commits the partial `agentMessage` with `cutOff: true` and fails the turn.
The Muse runtime ignored the mark: `consumeTurn` built the assistant message with the default `stopReason: "stop"`, so
OpenClaw delivered half an answer as an ordinary completed reply with nothing signalling it was incomplete.

## Why This Change Was Made

`extensions/muse/src/events.ts` now maps the mark onto the transport field the host already understands:
`assistantMessage(params, …, item.cutOff === true ? "length" : "stop")`.

No new contract and no core change: the host already treats `stopReason: "length"` as an incomplete reply
(`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/settled-turn-finalization.test.ts` exercises exactly that shape via
`cutOffAttempt`). MSP's own schema defines `Item.cutOff` as "the wire mark for the gate-off 'incomplete response'
rule", so carrying it is the documented intent rather than a new invention.

The text, the transcript bytes, and every other item kind are untouched; only the stop reason on a cut-off assistant
message changes.

## User Impact

A truncated Muse reply is now marked incomplete instead of being presented as the complete answer, so the existing
cut-off handling applies. Non-cut-off replies keep `stopReason: "stop"` exactly as before.

## Evidence

`extensions/muse/src/events.test.ts` gains a parameterised case (`cutOff=false` / `cutOff=true`) driving the real
`consumeTurn` with a folded `agentMessage` item and asserting the persisted message's `stopReason`.

## What Problem This Solves

`docs/tools/browser/troubleshooting.md` said that a Chromium lock naming another hostname stays unverified, but never
explained how to recover. On macOS with `scutil --get HostName` reporting `not set`, the host can flip between
`<name>.local` and `<name>.<router-domain>`; after that `openclaw browser start` fails with
`Chromium profile lock names another hostname` and the page offered no next step.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added a "Recovering from a stale lock" subsection next to that statement, covering exactly what the issue asked for:

- what the lock is — a `SingletonLock` symlink in `<config dir>/browser/<profile>/user-data` whose target is
  `<hostname>-<pid>`, and why OpenClaw ignores it when the hostname differs;
- how to confirm it is stale before deleting anything (`readlink` names the previous hostname and a PID; `ps -p` shows no
  such process; no other browser uses that profile);
- which entries to remove (`SingletonLock`, `SingletonSocket`, `SingletonCookie`) and that profile data — cookies,
  history, logins, preferences — is kept;
- how to prevent recurrence on macOS by pinning `sudo scutil --set HostName <stable-name>` and restarting the browser.

Every claim is checked against the implementation: `extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.ts` reads the lock target as
`<hostname>-<pid>` and returns "Chromium profile lock names another hostname" when the host differs, and the managed
profile directory is `path.join(CONFIG_DIR, "browser", profileName, "user-data")` with the default profile name
`openclaw`.

## User Impact

Docs only; no behavior change. Someone hitting the renamed-host lock now has a safe, ordered recovery instead of a dead end.

- `pnpm format:docs:check` → `Docs formatting clean (1420 files)`.
- `pnpm lint:docs` → `Summary: 0 issues in 0 files`.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`knowledge_grep` missed a Greek word when the saved body and the query used canonically equivalent spellings. Saving the
body as NFD (`α` + U+0301 + `λφα`) and querying the NFC form (`άλφα`) returned nothing, while the same query against the
NFC body returned the note. Stored text is unchanged between those cases, so a canonical-equivalent rewrite silently
changed which queries find a record.

## Why This Change Was Made

The keyword path is SQLite FTS5 with `tokenize='unicode61 remove_diacritics 2'`
(`extensions/knowledge/src/retrieval.ts`). `unicode61` does not unify canonically equivalent spellings — a decomposed
accent is a separate codepoint run from its composed form — so the index held a different token sequence than the
query.

Index and query text are now NFC-normalized before they reach FTS:

- both index writers (the persistent corpus and the query-local temporary corpus) normalize `title`, `aliases` and
  `body` on insert;
- `keywordExpression` normalizes the query before tokenizing.

Stored record bytes, hashes, revisions and lifecycle are untouched: normalization applies only to the FTS projection and
the query string. Accent-stripping behaviour (`remove_diacritics`) is unchanged — this only removes the NFC/NFD
difference the report described.

## User Impact

A note saved in either canonical spelling is found by a query in either spelling. Latin behaviour, unaccented queries,
ranking and pagination are unchanged; the existing retrieval suite still passes.

## Evidence

New test in `extensions/knowledge/src/retrieval.test.ts` using the existing service fixture (real storage, real FTS):

- a note whose body contains NFD `α` + U+0301 + `λφα` is returned for both the NFC and the NFD query spelling;
- the test asserts the two spellings really are canonically equivalent and differ as strings, plus a Latin control note
  that must not match.

Red on base: reverting only `retrieval.ts` fails with `άλφα: expected [] to strictly equal [ 'nfd_note' ]`; with the change
the same test passes and the whole file reports `21 passed`.

- `oxlint` on both touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- Test lines carry an allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/knowledge-nfc-keyword-match.txt`.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

comment.body:
Closing this: #195092 covers the same fix and also updates `docs/plugins/knowledge/retrieval.md`, which the report
explicitly asked for ("at minimum, the current unqualified accent-matching documentation should identify the actual
supported scope"). Broader coverage wins; no objection.

Two things from this attempt that may be useful there:

**1. The base failure, verbatim.** With the FTS writers and `keywordExpression` un-normalized, a note whose body holds
NFD `α` + U+0301 + `λφα` is not found by the NFC query:

```
AssertionError: άλφα: expected [] to strictly equal [ 'nfd_note' ]
```

Adding `normalize("NFC")` to the query expression alone is not enough — the mismatch is between the indexed token stream
and the query, so both writers (`reconcileKeywordIndex`'s insert and `temporaryCorpus`'s insert) and
`keywordExpression` need it. My version normalized `title`, `aliases` and `body` on insert and the query before
tokenizing, and left stored bytes, hashes and lifecycle untouched; the full `retrieval.test.ts` then reports 21 passed.

**2. The table that actually matters.** `reconcileKeywordIndex` and `temporaryCorpus` share `FTS_COLUMNS`, so a fix that
only touches one of them passes `knowledge_grep` but still misses on the query-local corpus used by scoped search. Worth
asserting both paths if you have not already.

My branch and worktree are gone; the test shape above is yours to reuse if helpful.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a Muse turn failed because a quota ran out, the harness replaced the turn error with
`new Error(turnError.message)` and then wrapped it as `new Error("Muse Code: …")` with no `cause`. MSP's typed
`TurnError.quota` field — the contract's way of saying "this was the quota class" — was dropped, so the host had to
guess from wording. Messages like `quota exhausted` or `Tier limit reached` do not classify as a rate limit, so a
configured fallback model never ran and the user got no reply.

## Why This Change Was Made

`extensions/muse/turn-failure.ts` now owns the mapping:

- `museTurnFailureError` throws `MuseQuotaLimitError` (status `429`) whenever `turnError.quota` is present, keeping the
  message and appending the reset instant when `resetsAtMs` is set;
- the `authRequired` sign-in message and the plain-message fallback are unchanged;
- the harness terminal failure now wraps the formatted message with `{ cause: failure }`, so the typed error stays
  reachable for `describeFailoverError`, which classifies through `cause`.

This follows the existing Codex precedent (`CodexUsageLimitPromptError` also carries `status = 429`) and MSP's rule to
branch on the presence of `quota`, never on the wording. The mapping moved out of `harness.ts` so that file (already over
the line cap) does not grow — the change actually shrinks it by 5 lines.

## User Impact

A Muse quota failure now classifies as a rate limit, so the configured fallback model runs instead of the user getting no
reply. The reset instant is visible in the message. Sign-in and plain-failure messages are unchanged, and nothing about
session state or stored records changes.

## Evidence

New `extensions/muse/turn-failure.test.ts` (4 tests, real `describeFailoverError`, no mocks):

- `quota` present → `MuseQuotaLimitError` with `status === 429`, message keeps Muse's detail and renders the reset instant;
- the wrapped terminal error (`new Error("Muse Code: …", { cause })`) keeps that `429` reachable through `cause`, which is
  what `describeFailoverError` walks to classify `rate_limit`;
- wording alone (exactly what the harness produced before) carries no typed status for the host to read;
- `authRequired` still points at `muse login`, and plain messages pass through unchanged.

`oxlint` on all three touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors. Test lines carry an allocation in
`config/test-lines-allocations/muse-quota-failover.txt`.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report and the MSP schema; the author reviewed the change and its
evidence.

Closing this: it is superseded by the merged #195148 (`fix(muse): quota and sign-in failures end with no reply`,
merged 2026-11-08T11:02Z), which reached the same outcome in the same file.

Verified on current `main`: `extensions/muse/harness.ts:518-531` now reads `turnError.quota`, builds the message from
`limitKind` and `resatsAtMs`, and passes `{ status: 429 }` for the quota case — the classification this PR also aimed at
(the merged version keeps it in `harness.ts` rather than a separate mapping module).

No objection to that shape; a separate module was only my way of keeping `harness.ts` under its line cap. Two small

- the wrapper error is the one the host classifies, so `status` has to survive it — either by attaching the status to the

- a quota reset far in the future (`resetsAtMs` in 2030) is what surfaced #195184: the host's rate-limit notice still

With the fix merged and the follow-up filed as #195184, there is nothing left for this branch. Closing.

Answering the intent question first, since it decides whether the change is even allowed to look like this.

**What the change does and does not touch.** `excludeFromContext` / `__openclaw.contextFreeCommand` are untouched: every

issue.body:
Closes #193534

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw config get/set/unset agents.entries.work...` cannot address an agent entry stored under a mixed-case key (`Work`) even though `openclaw agents list` shows it by its normalized id (`work`). `config get` reports the path valid but unset, `config set` tries to create a second `work` key and is declined with the duplicate-id error, and `config unset` reports the path not found.

## User Impact

User impact: the agent id that `agents list` prints now addresses the stored entry through `config get/set/unset/patch`, and the stored key keeps its spelling. Exact keys still win, hand-edited configs with casing-colliding keys keep their duplicate-id validation error, and ids that differ beyond casing (`work!`, `!!!`) remain unresolvable instead of silently hitting another agent.

## Why This Change Was Made

The config CLI used the `agents.entries.<id>` segment as a literal object key while the schema accepts keys case-insensitively and the runtime identifies entries by normalized id. `resolveStoredAgentsEntryKey` (in `config-cli-roster.ts`) rewrites the key segment to its stored spelling when the requested key is absent and exactly one stored key differs only by casing. The mutation runner resolves stored casing before checking whether a conditional write would redirect. If it would, the command rejects the write and leaves the config untouched. `config get` resolves the stored key before lookup while schema diagnostics use the authored path. A delete-then-write across casings in one patch still renames, because the second write only resolves when the stored key is gone.

## Evidence

- Integration tests in `src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts`: `set`/`get`/`unset` through `agents.entries.work...` edit the stored `Work` entry in place (key spelling preserved, no duplicate id); `unset` of ids that differ beyond casing (`agents.entries["!!!"].name`, `agents.entries.work!.name`) still fails with the path-not-found error and leaves the config untouched. `node scripts/test-projects.mts src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts` — 23/23 passing.
- Sibling suites: `config-cli.test.ts` (14), `config-cli.integration.test.ts` (25), `config-cli-input.test.ts` + `config-cli-path.test.ts` + `config-cli-runner.supplied-intent.test.ts` (91 combined) all passing.
- The current hosted [CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42094185967/job/127503921692) passed.
- The 34 added test lines have a matching allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/config-mixed-case-agents-entry-key.txt`.
- The gateway `agents.delete` sibling gap (#190496) is intentionally untouched; this PR scopes the fix to the config CLI surfaces named in the issue.


## Real CLI behavior proof

Run from source (`node --import tsx src/entry.ts`) with isolated `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` holding `{"agents":{"ownership":"explicit","entries":{"main":{},"Work":{"name":"Work Agent"}}}}`.

**Unpatched base, identical inputs:**

```
$ openclaw config get agents.entries.work.name
Config path is valid but unset: agents.entries.work.name. ...
$ openclaw config set agents.entries.work.name '"Renamed"' --strict-json
Config change declined. No settings were saved.
Config validation failed: agents.entries.work: agents.entries keys "Work" and "work" resolve to the same agent id "work"; ...
$ openclaw config unset agents.entries.work.name
Config path not found: agents.entries.work.name. Nothing was changed.
# saved agents.entries: {"main":{},"Work":{"name":"Work Agent"}}  (unchanged)
```

**This patch, identical inputs:**

```
$ openclaw config get agents.entries.work.name
Work Agent
$ openclaw config set agents.entries.work.name '"Renamed"' --strict-json
Updated agents.entries.work.name. Change will apply without restarting the gateway.
# saved agents.entries: {"main":{},"Work":{"name":"Renamed"}}   ← stored key keeps "Work"
$ openclaw config unset agents.entries.work.name
Removed agents.entries.work.name. Change will apply without restarting the gateway.
# saved agents.entries: {"main":{},"Work":{}}
$ openclaw config set agents.entries.work.name '"Renamed"' --strict-json --expect-current-json '"Work Agent"'

```

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The materialized session-archive read cache had an age-only policy: entries expired after 24 h, and nothing bounded
how many entries or bytes could exist before then. One archive-reading pass materializes **every** archive, so a host
whose `/tmp` is a small tmpfs filled it from a read cache alone (495 decompressed copies, 623 MB, on a 1 GiB tmpfs),
and the copies stayed for a day.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/config/sessions/archive-compression.ts` now enforces a budget alongside the TTL:

- `MATERIALIZED_ARCHIVE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 64` and `MATERIALIZED_ARCHIVE_CACHE_MAX_BYTES = 256 MiB`.
- `sweepMaterializedArchiveCache` keeps the TTL pass, then evicts least-recently-read entries (oldest `mtimeMs` first)
  until both bounds hold. A miss re-materializes a single archive, so the stalest entries are the cheapest to lose.
- The budget is applied **after each write**, not only on the interval sweep: one reading pass can materialize every
  archive inside a single sweep interval, which is exactly how the reported cache grew. With the cache bounded, the
  walk that enforces it stays cheap.

Source-identity validation is unchanged: cached bytes still only serve while the source archive's size and mtime match,
and eviction simply forces a fresh materialization.

## User Impact

A deployment with a small `/tmp` no longer has its temp filesystem consumed by archive reads; the cache keeps the most
recently read archives within 64 entries / 256 MiB and re-materializes the rest on demand. Archive reads and their
content are unchanged.

## Evidence

- New regression in `src/config/sessions/archive-compression.test.ts` (real `zstdCompressSync` archives, real
  materialization, cache root redirected to a temp dir):
  - materializing 80 distinct archives leaves at most 64 cache entries and at most 256 MiB on disk.
- Red on base: with the production change reverted, the same test fails (`1 failed | 5 passed`, 80 entries observed);
  with the fix, all 6 pass.
- `oxlint` on both files: 0 warnings, 0 errors. The added test lines carry an allocation in
  `config/test-lines-allocations/session-archive-cache-budget.txt`.
- The wider `src/config/sessions` suite is too large to finish inside this environment's per-command timeout; the
  archive cache has no other test consumers (`materializeSessionArchiveForRead` is referenced only by this test file).

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance (an agent working from the issue report); the author reviewed the change and its
evidence.

comment.body:
Closing this: the review found a real regression in my own change.

**The P1 is valid.** An archive that decompresses to more than the 256 MiB retained budget is deleted by the sweep
immediately after it is published, because my eviction loop does not exempt the file it just wrote. The caller then
receives a path that no longer exists: history indexing returns nothing and header discovery hits ENOENT, even though
the compressed source never changed. That is worse than the unbounded cache the PR set out to fix.

The other findings follow from the same shortcut:

- `.tmp` files of in-flight materializations are in the survivor inventory, so one writer's forced sweep can unlink
  another writer's open temp file and turn its `renameSync` into ENOENT.
- Cursor-based continuation (`ArchivedTranscriptReader.readSourcePage`) resumes from `cursor.path` without
  rematerializing, so evicting a page's plaintext between pages throws "Transcript archive changed during source
  pagination" for an unchanged archive.
- Sorting by `mtime` measures materialization time, not read recency, so cache hits never refresh their position.
- The mocked cache root starts empty and is only assigned inside the new test, so the earlier materialization tests were
  writing into a relative directory under the checkout. (The mock factory itself is fixed on the current head.)

**What a correct change looks like**: an entry cap that never evicts an oversized-but-valid entry, excluding temp
files, reader-side rematerialization when a cursor's plaintext is gone (or a retained lifetime tied to active readers),
and access-recency tracking that does not disturb transcript identity. That is a reader/cache lifecycle change rather
than a bounded sweep, so I would rather hand #193193 back than land a cache that can delete a valid archive's plaintext
out from under its reader.

## What Problem This Solves

The Matrix credentials store opened under a caller env's `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` while capture-based reads resolved the
state dir through the installed plugin runtime, so a freshly saved credential could be written to one database and read
from another. On Windows this currently fails `extensions/matrix/src/actions.credentials.test.ts`: the test harness pins
`OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` per worker while the pinned test runtime resolves its own dir, so the account reads
`configured: false` and sends prepare `null` right after a successful registration.

## Why This Change Was Made

`matrixCredentialsStoreOptions` let an explicit `env.OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` win over the installed runtime resolver. The
read path already treats the runtime as the locality owner: `captureMatrixCredentialsEnv` resolves through
`getOptionalMatrixRuntime()?.state.resolveStateDir(env)`. The store therefore now does the same when a runtime is
installed, and keeps the caller env override only when there is no runtime.

With the bundled production runtime nothing changes, because its resolver honors the env override; the fix removes the
divergence for runtimes that pin their own state dir, which is exactly where writes and reads previously disagreed.

## User Impact

A Matrix credential registered through the plugin is visible to account resolution and message sends in the same run, in
test harnesses and any host whose runtime resolver owns state locality. No configuration, storage format, or credential
content changes.

## Evidence

- New `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/credentials-read.test.ts`:
  - the store's resolved `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` equals the one `captureMatrixCredentialsEnv` produces for the same env;
  - the installed runtime's state dir wins over a caller override;
  - without a runtime, the caller override still applies.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`diagnostics.otel` had no deadline of its own for the provider shutdowns in `stopStarted`. With an OTLP endpoint that
refused connections (a sidecar collector receiving SIGTERM at the same time as the Gateway), `meterProvider.shutdown()`
waited on the exporter's own `timeoutMillis` (10s default) while retrying the refused connection, so the process left
about 11s after SIGTERM instead of ~2s, and the plugin-services shutdown grace expired with a warning:

```
[shutdown] plugin-services runtime disposal exceeded 5000ms; continuing shutdown
[shutdown] completed in 9921ms with warnings: plugin-services
```

The final flush cannot deliver anything once the collector is gone, so it should not hold the process.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bound the provider flush instead of removing it: `settleStopsWithinDeadline` races the three provider `shutdown()`
calls against a 1.5s deadline and reports a timeout the same way it already reports shutdown failures. The timer is
unref'd so it never keeps the event loop alive, and the deadline runs through the existing failure plumbing
(`retireExporterRoutes`, error aggregation), so an over-running flush stays visible rather than being silently dropped.

This keeps the normal path unchanged: providers that settle quickly still settle, and real shutdown errors still
surface. Only a flush that would outlive the gateway's grace period is cut short.

## User Impact

Operators running the Gateway beside an OpenTelemetry collector (sidecar/pod rollout) get a fast shutdown instead of a
~8s stall and a `plugin-services` warning. The last metric/trace/log batch was already undeliverable in that scenario,
so nothing that would have been delivered is lost.

## Evidence

- New test `service-shutdown-deadline.test.ts`:
  - fast stops settle and still report their failures;
  - a provider whose `shutdown()` never settles resolves within the deadline and reports
    `diagnostics-otel provider shutdown exceeded 20ms`.
- Bidirectional: with the pre-fix behavior (plain `Promise.allSettled` over the provider stops) the second test never
  finishes and the vitest shard is killed by the 120s runner timeout; with the fix it passes in 31ms.
- `oxlint` on both touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- Full shutdown path still exercised by the existing `diagnostics-otel` suites in CI.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance (an agent working from the issue report); the author reviewed the change and
its evidence.

comment.body:
Closing this: the review is right that the patch does not repair the defect it aims at.

**Why the approach falls short**

- Racing the three `shutdown()` promises only bounds *this* helper's wait. The OTLP `RetryingTransport` keeps referenced retry timers and the metric reader can still be awaiting its final export, so natural process exit can stay delayed by the original retries. The fix has to bound the exporter work itself (for example by giving the OTLP exporters a short `timeoutMillis`, which is the second option in the issue), not the await around it.
- `stopStarted` also serves config reloads, where a healthy collector may legitimately need more than 1.5s. An unconditional deadline turns that into a cleanup failure and pushes a diagnostics-only change into Gateway recovery.
- The race drops failures already observed before the deadline, because `Promise.allSettled` never delivers its result to the losing branch.

**What a correct fix looks like**

1. Bound the exporter/transport work (exporter-level timeout or transport shutdown) so retry timers stop holding the loop.
2. Keep reload cleanup joined and unbounded; apply any deadline only to the real shutdown path.
3. Aggregate already-settled provider failures together with the deadline failure.
4. Exercise the deadline through `createDiagnosticsOtelService().stop()` instead of a helper export, and include a real Gateway SIGTERM trace with the collector unavailable.

That is a design change across the plugin lifecycle and the pinned OTLP transport rather than a local guard, so I would rather hand #192086 back than keep a partial fix in review. Thanks for the detailed read; the analysis here should make the next attempt quicker.

Remote-mode iMessage attachments whose filename contains non-ASCII characters reached the recipient with the base name destroyed: `中文文件名测试（出站验证）.txt` arrived as `_-.txt` and an all-CJK `.doc` arrived as `.doc`. The remote staging path built its scp target with core's `sanitizeTempFileName`, whose `[^A-Za-z0-9._-]` rule collapses every non-ASCII run to hyphens and then trims them from the edges.

- Problem: the remote copy's filename was reduced to a bare extension for non-ASCII names.
- Solution: the iMessage staging path builds its own segment that keeps letters and digits from any script and neutralises only what a remote scp path must not carry.
- Changed: `extensions/imessage/src/remote-file.ts` (`buildRemoteStagingFileName`), plus coverage in the existing remote-file suite.
- Not changed: core's `sanitizeTempFileName`. Other callers keep the strict ASCII rule; only this staging path needed the wider charset.

The receiver gets its display name from the file it is handed, so the staging name is the user-visible name. macOS/APFS and the transport handle UTF-8 (the report's native `imsg send` control proves it), which makes ASCII-only staging an OpenClaw-side limitation rather than a transport constraint.

Names that collapse to nothing fall back to `attachment`, and over-long names are truncated while keeping their extension.

## User Impact

A CJK, accented or emoji-named document now arrives with a recognisable name instead of `.doc` or `_-.txt`. ASCII names stage exactly as before, and injected shell metacharacters are still removed.

issue.body:
Fixes #189447

## What Problem This Solves

When a release bumps `MEMORY_CHUNKING_VERSION`, the index identity becomes `mismatched` with `versionOrder: "older"`, so `shouldRepairIdentity` is true and the search runs the whole rebuild inline through `syncAdmitted`. Only after that does the code reach the `formatUpgradePendingKeywordOnly` check that would have answered from the existing keyword rows. On a real index the rebuild outlives the 30 s `memory_search` deadline, so the first search after an upgrade returns nothing even though the keyword index was usable.

- Problem: a chunking-version-only mismatch rebuilt inline before the keyword-only path could answer.
- Solution: answer from the keyword rows immediately and hand the upgrade to the existing search-maintenance owner, so the index still reaches the current format.
- Changed: `manager-search-orchestration.ts` hoists `formatUpgradePendingKeywordOnly` above the repair decision, excludes that case from the inline repair, and schedules `syncPublishedIndexInBackground` for it.
- Not changed: which identities are repairable, the keyword-only eligibility rules, the maintenance pipeline itself, and the existing "rebuild is pending" log.

## Why This Change Was Made

The keyword-only path already existed and is the right answer for a format-only upgrade: the rows are still lexically valid, so rebuilding before serving throws away the only deadline the caller has. Moving the existing predicate above the repair decision reuses that owner instead of adding a second eligibility rule.

Skipping the inline rebuild alone would strand the upgrade — the background-sync gate excludes the same identity, so an unchanged corpus would stay keyword-only forever. The pending-format branch therefore starts the same maintenance pass a dirty search would, reusing the in-flight set so repeated searches cannot stack rebuilds. Any mismatch that is not keyword-only still repairs inline as before.

## User Impact

The first `memory_search` after a chunking-version upgrade returns keyword results inside the deadline instead of timing out empty, and the index still upgrades in the background without a second search. Searches on a non-upgraded index, and upgrades that also change source or scope, behave exactly as before.

## Evidence

Two regression tests, both bidirectional and both run for real. Production changes reverted with the tests kept:

```text

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search-orchestration.test.ts -t "chunking version moved"
→ PASS: serves keyword rows instead of rebuilding when only the chunking version moved
node … -t "hands a pending format upgrade"
→ PASS: keyword answer plus a search-maintenance pass for the same identity

# production file reverted
→ FAIL: expected false to be true            (inline rebuild ran first)
→ FAIL: maintenance never entered            (no repair was handed off)

# full suite on the fixed tree
→ 21 passed
```

The tests drive the real manager: they sync a real index, rewrite the persisted `chunkingVersion` to the previous version through the fixture's own database handle, and then assert both the keyword answer and that maintenance was actually acquired for the pending upgrade.

Not covered here: the 30 s deadline itself on a multi-gigabyte production index, and completion of the background rebuild against a live embedding provider. Both need a live provider and a large corpus.

- Problem: recoverable shell-download failures were handled as manual-only.
- Solution: a recognized stale shell-download error schedules the existing guarded recovery from the error surface itself.
- Changed: `ui/src/app/app-shell-loader.tsx` wires `scheduleStaleChunkReload` the way `router-outlet.tsx` already does, and `ui/src/app/boot-composer.ts` registers a reload guard while unsent boot text exists.

`router-outlet.tsx` already renders an automatic `scheduleStaleChunkReload()` for recognized route errors, and the shell loader had the same primitive available but connected only to Retry. Reusing that owner keeps loop bounds in one place.

That reuse also exposes one hazard: the boot composer from #188153 keeps early text only in its own textarea, so a document reload before the route adopts it would discard what the operator typed. The guard therefore lives at the text's lifecycle owner — `boot-composer.ts` blocks reloads while it holds non-empty text and releases the block when a pane takes the draft. A failed recovery still lands on the error surface with manual Reload available.

## User Impact

A source-backed Control UI preview that hits a transient shell module download failure now recovers without a click. If the operator has already typed into the boot composer, the automatic reload is held instead of discarding that text. When recovery cannot proceed (unreachable, guard tripped), behavior is unchanged.

Bidirectional, each run real. Production behavior reverted with the tests kept:

```text
→ FAIL: expected true to be false (reload stayed allowed while text existed)

# both restored
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/app/boot-composer.test.ts ui/src/app/app-shell-loader.test.tsx
→ 2 files passed, 8 tests passed
```

Not proven: a live browser session against a real development server that aborts one shell request. That end-to-end run is the remaining gap; the tests above drive the same components and the same shared recovery function.

The implementer understands the code: the shared recovery owns reachability and loop bounds, the boot composer owns its unsent text, and neither surface should reload past the other's guard.
